solution.concept_anchor: AIFI refinancing powers — NABARD/NHB vs EXIM direct lending

statement_analysis.statement: NABARD primarily refinances commercial banks and cooperative banks for agriculture and rural development lending.
statement_analysis.reason: Refinancing commercial banks is NABARD's primary channel — it provides concessional refinance to banks extending credit to the agricultural and rural sector.

statement_analysis.statement: NHB (National Housing Bank) primarily refinances housing finance companies and commercial banks for housing loans.
statement_analysis.reason: NHB's core function is refinancing housing finance companies (HFCs) and banks — it is the apex institution for housing finance in India.

statement_analysis.statement: EXIM Bank primarily refinances commercial banks for export credit, similar to the model followed by NABARD for agricultural lending.
statement_analysis.reason: EXIM Bank primarily lends directly to exporters, foreign buyers, governments, and financial institutions — it does not primarily operate as a refinancer of commercial banks unlike NABARD.

statement_analysis.statement: SIDBI can both refinance commercial banks and NBFCs for MSME lending AND directly lend to MSME units.
statement_analysis.reason: SIDBI operates a dual-channel model — it refinances banks/NBFCs for MSME credit AND provides direct assistance to MSME units, unlike EXIM Bank which does not primarily refinance.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students may confuse EXIM Bank's two-tier MSME support model (lending to banks/NBFCs for on-lending to export MSMEs) with its primary lending character, and mark Statement 3 as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NABARD refinances commercial/cooperative banks for agricultural credit — unambiguously correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: NHB refinances HFCs and banks for housing loans — definitional, correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: 'EXIM Bank primarily refinances commercial banks for export credit like NABARD' — EXIM Bank primarily lends directly, not primarily as a refinancer; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 4: SIDBI dual model (refinance + direct lending) — correct; three of four are correct, select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses an entity-swap between EXIM Bank and NABARD — attributing NABARD's refinancing-first model to EXIM Bank. EXIM Bank does have some refinancing activity (for MSME export credit through banks) but its primary mode is direct lending to exporters and foreign counterparties. The swap makes Statement 3 appear plausible to students who recall EXIM Bank's two-tier MSME lending model.
solution.final_explanation:
The four AIFIs have distinct primary operating models — some are predominantly refinancers, others are primarily direct lenders.

• Statement 1 — Correct: NABARD's primary function is refinancing commercial banks, cooperative banks, and RRBs for agricultural and rural development credit.
• Statement 2 — Correct: NHB refinances housing finance companies (HFCs) and commercial banks for home loans — it is the apex institution for housing finance.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: EXIM Bank primarily lends directly — to Indian exporters, foreign buyers, governments, and financial institutions. It is not a refinancer of commercial banks for export credit in the manner NABARD operates. Its two-tier MSME model (through banks/NBFCs) is a secondary channel, not the primary model.
• Statement 4 — Correct: SIDBI uniquely combines refinancing (to banks/NBFCs) with direct lending to MSME units — a dual-channel approach.

Three of four statements are correct.

Value Addition:
• The refinancing vs. direct lending distinction is a recurring UPSC comparator between AIFIs.
• EXIM Bank's direct lending to foreign governments and entities is what makes it unique — no other AIFI has this cross-border direct lending mandate.
• NHB's refinancing role became more prominent after the IL&FS crisis highlighted liquidity stress in HFCs.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may confuse Buyer's Credit (loan to foreign buyer) with Supplier's Credit (loan to Indian exporter who then extends credit) — both involve deferred payment but differ in who receives the loan and who bears risk.
elimination_logic: Match Buyer's Credit: EXIM Bank lends to the foreign buyer — risk on foreign entity; matches description 2.
Match Supplier's Credit: EXIM Bank lends to the Indian exporter who extends deferred credit to the foreign buyer — risk on Indian entity; matches description 4.
Match Performance Guarantee: assures the foreign party that the Indian exporter will complete the contract — matches description 1.
Match Financial Guarantee: assures repayment to the foreign lender/buyer — matches description 3; confirm option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap swaps Buyer's Credit and Supplier's Credit descriptions — both involve deferred payment export financing but the loan direction and risk-bearer differ fundamentally. Students who recall 'Buyer's Credit = deferred payment' without remembering who receives the loan will conflate it with Supplier's Credit, leading to an incorrect match.
solution.final_explanation:
EXIM Bank's four key instruments — Buyer's Credit, Supplier's Credit, Performance Guarantee, and Financial Guarantee — each have distinct mechanics and risk profiles.

Correct matches:
• A–2 (Buyer's Credit): EXIM Bank lends directly to the foreign buyer; the foreign entity repays EXIM Bank; risk sits on the foreign entity.
• B–4 (Supplier's Credit): EXIM Bank lends to the Indian exporter, who then extends deferred payment terms to the foreign buyer; risk sits on the Indian exporter.
• C–1 (Performance Guarantee): EXIM Bank guarantees to the foreign party that the Indian exporter will fulfil contractual performance obligations — assures contract completion.
• D–3 (Financial Guarantee): EXIM Bank guarantees repayment to a foreign lender or buyer — assures that financial obligations will be met.

The common trap: confusing Buyer's Credit (foreign entity receives loan) with Supplier's Credit (Indian exporter receives loan).

Value Addition:
• Both Buyer's Credit and Supplier's Credit facilitate deferred payment exports — especially important for capital goods and project exports.
• Performance and financial guarantees are contingent liabilities — EXIM Bank may require counter-guarantees from Indian exporters before issuance.
• ECGC's guarantee direction (toward Indian banks) is the opposite of EXIM Bank's guarantee direction (toward foreign parties).

solution.concept_anchor: AIFI classification and appropriate regulatory framework for a new trade DFI
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the Banking Regulation Act 1949 is the most familiar financial regulation framework and students may assume any new financially active institution should fall under it.
elimination_logic: Identify what type of institution is being created: a government-owned institution for financing international trade — mirrors EXIM Bank's character exactly.
Eliminate (a): Banking Regulation Act 1949 applies to commercial and cooperative banks — a DFI for trade finance would not be regulated under this Act; incorrect.
Eliminate (c): RBI Act Second Schedule inclusion is for commercial banks accepting public deposits — a trade DFI would not be listed here; incorrect.
Eliminate (d): NABARD Act framework applies to agriculture/rural — not relevant for trade finance; incorrect.
Select (b): The correct approach is a special enabling Act of Parliament that creates the institution as a statutory body, with RBI supervision as an AIFI — exactly the EXIM Bank model; option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a partial-truth trap — the Banking Regulation Act is a real financial regulation statute but it is designed for deposit-taking commercial banks, not for development finance institutions. The scenario tests whether students can apply the EXIM Bank model (special Act + AIFI classification) to a hypothetical new institution, rather than defaulting to the most familiar regulatory framework.
solution.final_explanation:
When a government wishes to create a dedicated institution for international trade finance, the EXIM Bank model provides the institutional template — a special statutory body with AIFI classification, not a commercial bank.

Application of principle: EXIM Bank was established under a special Act of Parliament (not the Companies Act or Banking Regulation Act), classified as an AIFI under RBI supervision, and exempted from CRR/SLR requirements. A new trade DFI would follow this template.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Banking Regulation Act 1949 governs deposit-taking commercial banks. A government-owned trade DFI would not be regulated under this Act since it would not accept public deposits.
• Option (b) — Correct: A special enabling Act of Parliament creates the institution as a statutory body; RBI classifies and supervises it as an AIFI; CRR/SLR exemptions apply since it is not a deposit-taking commercial bank.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Second Schedule inclusion is for scheduled commercial banks — a trade DFI would not qualify for or require this classification.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NABARD's legislative framework is for agriculture/rural development — not the appropriate model for a trade finance institution.

Value Addition:
• The AIFI framework under RBI allows sectoral DFIs to operate with tailored prudential norms.
• Special Acts of Parliament give statutory bodies specific powers (like equity participation or guarantee issuance) that Companies Act companies may not automatically have.
• The four current AIFIs cover agriculture, housing, MSMEs, and trade — any new sectoral DFI would likely follow the same template.

solution.concept_anchor: EXIM Bank two-tier MSME lending model — not direct retail
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because SIDBI does refinance commercial banks for MSME lending, which is an activity that also overlaps with EXIM Bank's two-tier model — students may mistake SIDBI for the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the shared category: channels through which EXIM Bank reaches export MSMEs — should be indirect/two-tier mechanisms.
Check (a): Credit lines to commercial banks for on-lending to MSME exporters — this IS a two-tier mechanism; belongs to the group.
Check (b): Credit lines to NBFCs for on-lending to MSME exporters — also two-tier; belongs to the group.
Check (c): MSME cluster development financing in export-oriented geographic concentrations — this is a documented EXIM Bank activity; belongs to the group.
Check (d): EXIM Bank directly lending to individual MSME export units as a retail lender — EXIM Bank does NOT do this; it is not a retail lender to individual MSMEs; this is the ODD ONE OUT.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) exploits a scope-extension trap by presenting EXIM Bank as a direct retail lender to individual MSMEs — which it is not. EXIM Bank uses a two-tier model exclusively for MSME outreach. The other three options all describe valid two-tier or indirect mechanisms. Students who know EXIM Bank supports MSMEs may not recall that it does so only through intermediaries, not directly.
solution.final_explanation:
EXIM Bank reaches MSME exporters through indirect, two-tier channels — not through direct retail lending to individual MSME units.

• Option (a): Credit lines to commercial banks for on-lending to MSME exporters — this is a valid two-tier EXIM Bank mechanism; belongs to the group.
• Option (b): Credit lines to NBFCs for on-lending to MSME exporters — also a two-tier channel; belongs to the group.
• Option (c): MSME cluster development financing in export-oriented geographic concentrations — EXIM Bank does finance geographic clusters of export-oriented MSMEs; belongs to the group.
• Option (d) — ODD ONE OUT: Direct retail lending to individual MSME export units. EXIM Bank is not a retail lender — it channels support through commercial banks and NBFCs, not directly to individual MSME borrowers.

Value Addition:
• SIDBI, by contrast, CAN lend directly to individual MSME units — this is a key differentiator from EXIM Bank's MSME approach.
• The two-tier model ensures wider reach while keeping EXIM Bank focused on wholesale/institutional financing.
• EXIM Bank's MSME support is export-specific — unlike SIDBI's broader MSME mandate covering both domestic and export-oriented units.

solution.concept_anchor: G20 Common Framework and EXIM Bank's African LOC exposure

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Debt distress in African nations that have borrowed through EXIM Bank's Lines of Credit affects India's position and negotiating leverage in multilateral debt restructuring forums such as the G20 Common Framework.
statement_analysis.reason: India's bilateral creditor status through EXIM Bank's LOC exposures directly engages India in G20 Common Framework negotiations — the scale of exposure determines India's negotiating position.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Under the G20 Common Framework, EXIM Bank's outstanding loan claims on distressed African nations are automatically written off to provide debt relief, without any recovery of principal by India.
statement_analysis.reason: The G20 Common Framework facilitates debt restructuring — not automatic write-offs. India negotiates terms including repayment rescheduling and haircuts, not unconditional write-offs.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both statements deal with G20 Common Framework and African debt, and students who know India participates in the Framework may mark both as correct without distinguishing between restructuring and write-off.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: EXIM Bank's LOC exposure in distressed African nations → India's position in G20 Common Framework — this causal link is accurate; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: 'Automatically written off without any recovery' — G20 Common Framework involves negotiated restructuring, not automatic write-offs; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a partial-truth trap — it correctly identifies the G20 Common Framework as the relevant mechanism but falsely characterizes the outcome as 'automatic write-offs.' Students who know about African debt distress and India's LOC exposure may not recall the precise mechanics of the G20 Common Framework (negotiated restructuring vs. write-off), making Statement 2 superficially plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
African debt distress has created real challenges for EXIM Bank's LOC portfolio recovery, engaging India in multilateral debt negotiations through the G20 Common Framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: EXIM Bank's bilateral LOC claims on distressed African nations make India a creditor in G20 Common Framework negotiations. The size of India's exposure directly affects its negotiating leverage and the restructuring terms it can influence or be pressured to accept.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: G20 Common Framework does not involve automatic write-offs. It provides a structured process for negotiating debt treatment — including repayment rescheduling, maturity extensions, and in some cases principal haircuts — but all of these are negotiated outcomes, not automatic concessions. India retains recovery rights through the restructuring process.

Value Addition:
• Zambia and Ethiopia are among the first countries to enter the G20 Common Framework for debt treatment — both have EXIM Bank exposure.
• India's participation in G20 Common Framework as a bilateral creditor is a novel diplomatic role that has become more prominent since 2020.
• Debt restructuring outcomes can affect EXIM Bank's NPA recognition and provisioning in subsequent financial years.

solution.concept_anchor: EXIM Bank operational commencement and IDBI handover
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students may recall the EXIM Bank Act was 1981 and EXIM Bank commenced operations in 1982 but then confuse whether IDBI's international operations were handed over before or after EXIM Bank's commencement.
elimination_logic: Anchor 1: EXIM Bank Act enacted — 1981 (legislative foundation must precede operations).
Anchor 2: EXIM Bank commenced operations — March 1, 1982 (the Act must precede commencement).
Anchor 3: EXIM Bank took over international financing from IDBI — this happened upon commencement in 1982, simultaneously with or immediately after Anchor 2.

Anchor 4: ECGC established — ECGC was established in 1957, predating EXIM Bank by over two decades; chronologically ECGC → EXIM Act → EXIM commencement + IDBI handover — option (d) with ECGC first is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places ECGC's establishment after EXIM Bank in some options. ECGC was established in 1957 — long before EXIM Bank (1982). Students who know ECGC and EXIM Bank are contemporary export promotion institutions may not recall that ECGC is actually much older, predating EXIM Bank by 25 years.
solution.final_explanation:
The chronology of India's export finance and insurance institutions reveals important sequencing that is frequently confused in Prelims.

Correct sequence:
1. ECGC established (1957) — India's first export credit insurance institution, created over two decades before EXIM Bank.
2. EXIM Bank Act enacted (1981) — Parliament creates the legislative foundation.
3. EXIM Bank commences operations and takes over IDBI's international financing (March 1, 1982) — both events occur at commencement.

Why wrong options fail:
• Options placing ECGC after EXIM Bank confuse contemporaneous export promotion institutions with their actual founding dates.
• Options placing EXIM Bank commencement before the 1981 Act are logically impossible — a statutory body cannot operate before its enabling legislation.
• The IDBI handover is simultaneous with or immediately follows EXIM Bank's March 1982 commencement — not a separate later event.

Value Addition:
• ECGC (est. 1957) predates EXIM Bank (est. 1982) by 25 years — one of the oldest Indian export promotion institutions.
• IDBI was established in 1964 and handled international trade financing until EXIM Bank took over in 1982.
• The separation of functions — insurance (ECGC) vs. financing (EXIM) — reflects the specialization of India's export promotion architecture.

solution.concept_anchor: EXIM Bank green exports and defence export financing

statement_analysis.statement: EXIM Bank has extended financing to support exports of renewable energy equipment for overseas projects, reflecting its engagement with green export financing.
statement_analysis.reason: Green export financing — specifically for renewable energy equipment exported for overseas projects — is a documented emerging mandate of EXIM Bank.

statement_analysis.statement: EXIM Bank's financing of defence exports is prohibited under Indian law as defence production is classified as a strategic sector where private sector and financial institution involvement is disallowed.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no such prohibition — EXIM Bank actively finances defence exports under the Defence Export Policy 2020, and private sector participation in defence production has been significantly liberalized.

statement_analysis.statement: EXIM Bank has been mandated under the Foreign Trade Policy to replace ECGC as the primary credit insurance provider for Indian exporters in the pharmaceutical sector.
statement_analysis.reason: No such mandate exists — ECGC remains the credit insurance provider; EXIM Bank provides financing, not insurance, for pharmaceutical exports. This is a fabricated mandate.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students may consider whether all three statements are incorrect, especially if they are uncertain about green export financing being a real mandate.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Renewable energy equipment financing for overseas projects — this is a documented EXIM Bank green finance initiative; Statement 1 IS correct; exclude it from 'not correct'.
Check Statement 2: 'Defence export financing prohibited under Indian law' — Defence Export Policy 2020 explicitly promotes defence exports; EXIM Bank finances them; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 3: 'EXIM Bank mandated to replace ECGC as credit insurance provider' — no such mandate exists; EXIM Bank provides financing, not insurance; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are not correct → select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a scope-extension trap by invoking 'strategic sector' classification to invent a prohibition on EXIM Bank's defence financing role. Students who recall that defence was historically restricted may not know that the sector has been extensively liberalized and that the Defence Export Policy 2020 actively promotes EXIM Bank's role. Statement 3 is a plausible fabrication that conflates EXIM Bank (financing) with ECGC (insurance).
solution.final_explanation:
EXIM Bank's emerging mandates in green exports and defence are real but must be distinguished from fabricated institutional roles.

• Statement 1 — Correct: EXIM Bank does finance renewable energy equipment exports for overseas projects — an emerging green finance mandate aligned with India's climate commitments and export promotion goals.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no legal prohibition on EXIM Bank financing defence exports. The Defence Export Policy 2020 explicitly encourages defence exports, and EXIM Bank's financing role is part of this architecture. Defence sector liberalization has opened private sector and financial institution participation.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: EXIM Bank has not been mandated to replace ECGC as a credit insurance provider in any sector. EXIM Bank provides financing; ECGC provides credit insurance — these are distinct functions that remain with their respective institutions.

Value Addition:
• India's target of USD 5 billion in annual defence exports by 2025 makes EXIM Bank's defence financing role increasingly significant.
• Green export financing by EXIM Bank supports India's positioning in global renewable energy supply chains.
• Vaccine Maitri (pharmaceutical exports) and defence exports represent EXIM Bank's transition from pure trade finance toward strategic economic diplomacy financing.

solution.concept_anchor: LOC as soft power — EXIM Bank and India's foreign policy
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the soft power role of EXIM Bank's LOCs is well-known and students may instinctively assume that the infrastructure financing explains its soft power function, making both A and R appear causally linked.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes: EXIM Bank's LOCs function as a soft power instrument by financing infrastructure in partner nations, creating economic linkages and goodwill.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Yes: At least 75% of LOC contract value must be sourced from India — this is the Indian content conditionality.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? No: The 75% Indian content requirement explains why LOCs benefit Indian exporters (export promotion) — not why they function as soft power instruments. Soft power derives from the infrastructure financed and the developmental impact on the recipient nation, not from the sourcing conditionality. R describes the trade benefit; A describes the diplomatic benefit — they are related but R does not causally explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap here is subtle — the 75% Indian content rule (R) and soft power impact (A) are both true aspects of LOCs but the causal arrow runs in different directions. The content rule is about domestic export promotion; soft power derives from the development impact on partner nations. Students who see both as 'LOC features' may incorrectly assume one explains the other.
solution.final_explanation:
EXIM Bank's Lines of Credit serve dual purposes — export promotion and foreign policy — but these goals have different causal drivers.

Assertion (A): EXIM Bank's LOCs function as India's soft power instrument — by financing roads, railways, power plants, and other infrastructure in partner nations, India builds economic linkages and diplomatic goodwill. This is factually correct and is explicitly acknowledged in India's foreign policy discourse.

Reason (R): At least 75% of the contract value under EXIM Bank's LOCs must be sourced from India. This is also factually correct — the Indian content conditionality is a core feature of the LOC framework.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The 75% rule explains why LOCs benefit Indian exporters (trade/export promotion goal) — it is not the reason LOCs create soft power. Soft power derives from the recipient nation's experience of Indian-financed development — the development impact and project outcomes. R is about benefiting Indian industry; A is about benefiting India's diplomatic standing. The two are related but R is not the causal explanation for A.

Value Addition:
• India's soft power through LOCs is often compared to China's infrastructure diplomacy — though India's conditionalities and terms differ.
• Soft power through development financing creates long-term goodwill that may translate into diplomatic support in multilateral forums.
• The Indian content requirement creates domestic political support for EXIM Bank's LOC programme within India.
solution.correct_option_note: Option b confirmed — both A and R correct but R does not explain A.

statement_analysis.reason: There is no such exclusivity requirement in the EXIM Bank Act — while CAG may audit EXIM Bank, the claim of exclusive CAG audit with prohibition on private auditors is a fabricated provision.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because CAG audits government-owned entities and students may assume exclusive CAG jurisdiction applies to EXIM Bank, making all three statements appear correct.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible fabrication — it combines two real facts (CAG audits government entities; EXIM Bank is government-owned) into a false institutional requirement. Students who know CAG has audit jurisdiction over public institutions may assume this extends to exclusive audit rights, overlooking that most public financial institutions appoint statutory auditors through normal processes alongside or instead of CAG.
solution.final_explanation:
EXIM Bank's governance structure reflects its multi-stakeholder character and government ownership, but specific claims about audit exclusivity require careful verification.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The board includes RBI, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Commerce, FIEO, and independent directors — this multi-ministry and industry representation ensures diverse oversight of EXIM Bank's dual trade-finance mandate.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The MD & CEO is a government appointment — consistent with EXIM Bank's 100% GOI ownership and its character as a statutory body accountable to the executive.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No provision in the EXIM Bank Act mandates exclusive CAG audit with a prohibition on private chartered accountant firms. This is a fabricated restriction. Public sector financial institutions typically have statutory auditors appointed through RBI/GOI processes, which may or may not involve CAG.

Value Addition:
• EXIM Bank's accounts are placed before Parliament — a constitutional accountability mechanism separate from audit arrangements.
• FIEO representation ensures export industry voice in institutional governance — distinguishing EXIM Bank from purely government-controlled entities.
• RBI's presence on the board creates a link between monetary policy oversight and EXIM Bank's external trade finance operations.

solution.concept_anchor: EXIM Bank resource mobilization — bonds not deposits
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students may confuse NABARD's resource mobilization (which does include rural infrastructure development bonds and borrowings from NIDA — NABARD Infrastructure Development Assistance) with EXIM Bank's instruments.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): 'EXIM Bank — accepts fixed deposits from exporters as a primary resource mobilization channel' — EXIM Bank cannot accept public deposits; this pair is incorrect.
Evaluate (b): 'EXIM Bank — raises funds through bonds, commercial paper, and international borrowings, NOT through retail deposits' — both elements are accurate; this is a correctly matched pair.

Evaluate (c): 'NABARD — raises resources exclusively through government budget transfers and cannot borrow from capital markets' — NABARD issues bonds and borrows from capital markets; this pair is incorrect.
Evaluate (d): 'NHB — deposits from housing finance customers form its primary resource base' — NHB does not take customer deposits; it is a refinancing institution; this pair is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits an entity-swap between EXIM Bank and commercial banks — commercial banks accept fixed deposits; EXIM Bank cannot. Students who associate EXIM Bank with exporters may assume exporters can place deposits with it for trade purposes. Option (c) incorrectly describes NABARD as incapable of market borrowing — NABARD actively issues bonds and accesses capital markets.
solution.final_explanation:
AIFIs raise resources through different channels — all four are distinct from commercial banks in their inability or limited ability to accept public deposits.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: EXIM Bank does not accept fixed deposits from exporters or the general public. Retail deposit-taking requires scheduled commercial bank status, which EXIM Bank does not have.
• Option (b) — Correct: EXIM Bank mobilizes resources through domestic and international bonds, commercial paper, and borrowings from RBI and GOI. No public deposit window exists — this is a defining characteristic that distinguishes EXIM Bank from commercial banks.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: NABARD is not limited to government budget transfers. It actively issues bonds (NABARD bonds are well-known retail instruments) and borrows from capital markets, the GOI, and international institutions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NHB is a refinancing institution. It does not take deposits from housing finance customers — its resources come from borrowings and refinance operations.

Value Addition:
• EXIM Bank's multiple borrowing windows — RBI, GOI, domestic bonds, international bonds (including Masala Bonds) — give it flexible access to funds.
• NABARD bonds are eligible for SLR purposes — making them attractive to commercial banks.
• The prohibition on public deposits for AIFIs is a structural feature that preserves the wholesale character of development finance institutions.
